consensus_summary: Consensus identifies 'Gospel' primarily as the good news of salvation accomplished through Jesus Christ—especially his death for sins, burial, and resurrection—together with the related announcement of God's kingdom/reign, with the four canonical narratives as a common secondary literary sense.
book_summary: The book identifies the gospel as the good news of the coming kingdom in which the law goes forth from Zion, already proclaimed to Abraham and at Mount Sinai and renewed under Jesus' rule.
consensus_core_identification: Good news of salvation/God's saving reign through Christ's death, resurrection, and kingdom.
book_core_identification: Good news of the coming kingdom (law from Zion), proclaimed beforehand to Abraham and Sinai and renewed under Jesus.
boundary_disagreement: The book centers law-from-Zion / coming-kingdom content and treats Abrahamic and Sinai proclamations as definitional gospel preaching, while demoting the usual 1 Cor 15 death-burial-resurrection summary to a merely 'commonly taught' sense rather than the entry's core.
material_contradiction: None at the broad category of euangelion as saving good news tied to God's reign and Jesus; the disagreement is over defining content, historical occasions, and which biblical accent is primary.
rationale: Minimum cores share the general referent 'good news of God's kingdom/salvation associated with Jesus,' so this is not a full replacement or novelty. Consensus already lists kingdom-centered and Isaianic/Abrahamic strands as common. The book preserves that category but materially narrows and re-specifies it: primary content becomes the coming kingdom in which law goes from Zion; extension explicitly includes Sinai as gospel proclamation and does not take the Pauline atonement summary as the entry's definition (only as the noted common view). That is boundary/precision disagreement, i.e. REFINED, not MATCH or DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: Historic mainstream definitional texts (especially 1 Cor 15:1-4 and Romans 1:16) make Christ's death and resurrection the core content of the gospel, which the entry neither states nor treats as primary.
